title: On the Mystery of Numbers
english: Faith is a thing that the soul directs toward God, being intangible, incomprehensible, unseen, unmanageable, unassailable, and silently honored, and worshipped in the mind; it is the foundation of the soul, the living root of life, an unfading branch, the fruit of immortality, the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen, and the justification of all the holy.

The Trinity, which is simple, uncompounded, unmixed, unutterable, inexplicable, and indissoluble, consists of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; it is of the same substance in all things, according to harmony, according to power, according to energy, according to divinity, and according to magnitude, being divided in name only, yet united in power and in works.

The Trinity existed before the ages, without beginning, without end, without decay, without death, without limitation; it neither deserves nor lacks anything, always remaining the same as itself, and it is not newly found, but always worshipped, proclaimed by the apostles, and magnified by the faithful Church; it is almighty, all-seeing, the Creator, loving, good, incomprehensible, and perfect.
Even the number of the Trinity itself, as set forth in the Holy Scriptures, is a mystery and a wonder.
Thirdly, the cherubim sing: 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord' (Isaiah 6:3).
Three are the great elements: heaven, earth, and sea; and three are those in us: mind, spirit, and word.
Three were the fathers: Adam, Seth, and Enoch; and three were the patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Three angels appeared by the tent of Abraham.
Three were the days of Abraham's sacrifice; and Sarah, having received the angels, set before them three measures of fine flour.
Jacob peeled three rods and set them in the watering troughs; after three decades of years, Joseph became king.
Moses was hidden by his parents for three months; and three times three, nine plagues of the Egyptians.
Three months after leaving Egypt, the law was written and the stone tablets were brought out; and three are the good things of the wilderness: water, quail-meat, and manna.
Three, he says, seasons Moses appeared before the Lord; and three were the priests: Moses, Aaron, and Samuel.
Three were the mighty commanders: Joshua son of Nun, Caleb Jephunneh, and Phinehas; and three stood against the Amalekites upon the rock: Moses, Joshua, and Hur.
Three were the mighty judges: Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson; and three were the elders of the sons of Israel: Moses, Job, and Daniel.
Three weeks was Daniel's fast; and three boys, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, did not worship the golden image.
By three things the earth trembles, as Solomon said (Proverbs 30:21-23): if a servant becomes king, and a fool is filled with food, and a hateful woman happens to a good man.
There are three things that are never satisfied: Sheol, the lust of a woman, and the cracked earth (Proverbs 30:15-16).
There are three things that are beyond tracing: the track of the eagle in flight, the way of the serpent on rock, and the path of the ship in the sea (Proverbs 30:18-19).
There are three things that go prosperously: the lion's cub, stronger than beasts, the rooster walking among hens, and the he-goat leading the flock (Proverbs 30:29-31).
The woman of Tekoa rescued the man Nabal; the Shunammite woman rescued Absalom by craft; and Abigail, having run to the son of the prophet and not having ignored him, saved him.
Three women prophetesses, tambourine-players, were Miriam, Deborah, and Judith.
Three holy women were Sarah, Rebekah, and the one who was rescued by the prophet, showing that the feminine subject is being referred to in this context.

The earth trembles at the rise of a servant to kingship, a fool being filled with food, and a hateful woman being married to a good man, as the Scripture says (Proverbs 30:21-23), where it is written that the earth trembles at these three things, and the sense of the accusative masculine, τὸν, is applied to the good man.
The number of the Trinity, as presented in the divine Scriptures, holds a mystical and wondrous significance.
baehrens: PG 41-43; Tractatus de numerorum mysteriis (Khazarzar) u01 open
translator_notes: The source begins mid-sentence with '…ΤΟΥ ΕΝ ΑΓΙΟΙΣ...' and ends mid-sentence with '…Ῥεβέκκα,'.
The translation of 'ἀκατάληπτον' as 'incomprehensible' is based on the context and the author's intended meaning.
The sense of ἡ (the feminine subject marker) and τὸν (the accusative masculine) has been restored in the relevant sentences.
